data.title: Kimbell outlines more acquisitions after $360M in deals as Q2 distribution rises 15% to $0.47
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Kimbell Royalty Partners (KRP) Q2 2026

Management View

  • "To start off, we are pleased to report an outstanding quarter for Kimbell, which includes records for oil, natural gas and NGL revenues, net income, consolidated adjusted EBITDA, lease bonuses, average daily production and cash available for distribution." (Chairman of the Board & CEO Bob Ravnaas)

  • "We also closed on our previously announced Mesa Royalties acquisition in June" and "last month we announced the second drop-down acquisition since our IPO," with both transactions "expected to add meaningful production and drive cash flow growth for years to come." (CEO Ravnaas)

  • "Even with the uncertainty occurring across the broader geopolitical landscape in recent months, activity on our acreage remains robust with 91 rigs actively drilling at quarter-end, representing a market share of U.S. land rigs at 16%." (CEO Ravnaas)

  • "This record second quarter performance allowed us to declare a Q2 2026 distribution of $0.47 per common unit, up 15% from Q1 2026." (CEO Ravnaas)

  • "Oil, natural gas and NGL revenues totaled $103 million during the second quarter" and "second quarter average daily production was 25,830 BOE per day." (President & CFO Davis Ravnaas)

  • "Second quarter general and administrative expenses were $10.2 million, $5.9 million of which was cash G&A expense or $2.50 per BOE, below the midpoint of our guidance range." (CFO Ravnaas)

  • "At June 30, 2026, we had approximately $478.7 million in debt outstanding" and "net debt to trailing 12 months consolidated adjusted EBITDA of approximately 1.4x." (CFO Ravnaas)

Outlook

  • "Today we are also affirming our financial and operational guidance ranges for 2026" and "we can expect to update guidance upon the closing of the drop-down acquisition that was announced on July 17, 2026." (CFO Ravnaas)

  • "We remain confident about the prospects for continued development in 2026" tied to "the number of rigs actively drilling on our acreage, especially in the Permian, higher commodity prices as well as our line-of-sight wells exceeding our maintenance well count." (CFO Ravnaas)

  • Compared with Q1, management repeated similar oil-price and activity framing, while adding near-term timing language around the drop-down: "slated to close later this month." (CEO Ravnaas)

Financial Results

  • "Oil, natural gas and NGL revenues totaled $103 million" and "total second quarter consolidated adjusted EBITDA was a record $84.9 million." (CFO Ravnaas)

  • "We estimate that approximately 47% of this distribution is expected to be considered return on capital" and "the remaining 25% will be used to pay down a portion of the outstanding borrowings" on the revolver. (CFO Ravnaas)

  • "During the second quarter, we repurchased and canceled 500,000 units... for an aggregate purchase price of approximately $7.4 million at an average price of $14.70 per unit." (CFO Ravnaas)

  • "On June 24, 2026, we increased the borrowing base and aggregate commitments... from $625 million to $660 million." (CFO Ravnaas)

Q&A

  • Timothy Rezvan, KeyBanc Capital Markets Inc., Research Division: asked whether new acquisitions should support a "steady growth CAGR" profile; President & CFO Ravnaas responded, "The short answer to that, Tim, is yes," adding the company targets deals "immediately accretive to our cash flow and accretive to DCF over time" with "very similar growth and inventory characteristics." (CFO Ravnaas)

  • Timothy Rezvan, KeyBanc Capital Markets Inc., Research Division: pressed on liquidity and preferred units with the facility "over 70% drawn"; President & CFO Ravnaas said, "we would expect another increase in the borrowing base as a result of the drop-down," and on preferreds, "we want to be opportunistic on redeeming the preferred units" while keeping leverage conservative: "For a royalty company, we think 1.5x is low." (CFO Ravnaas)

  • Timothy Rezvan, KeyBanc Capital Markets Inc., Research Division: asked if Kimbell is ready to transact again; President & CFO Ravnaas described Permian competitiveness: "We've been on a couple of large marketed packages recently in the Permian and got absolutely destroyed" with "bids that were nearly 2x what we were paying," adding, "we're going to be very selective, and obviously, we're not going to overpay." (CFO Ravnaas)

  • Nicholas Armato, Texas Capital: asked about stronger lease bonuses and leasing interest; President & CFO Ravnaas linked it to prices and zones: "with the increase in oil prices and renewed interest in deeper zones... we have seen an uptick in lease bonus activity" and "we probably project that that will continue into subsequent quarters." (CFO Ravnaas)

  • Nicholas Armato, Texas Capital: asked how DUC/permit backlog trends after the drop-down; President & CFO Ravnaas said, "I would expect it to be the same" relative to maintenance needs, and added disclosure conservatism: "we only identify things that are discrete, that we know about." (CFO Ravnaas)

  • Paul Diamond, Citigroup Inc., Research Division: asked about basin-by-basin activity modulation; President & CFO Ravnaas said Permian rig count "quarter-over-quarter was up 23%" and Mid-Con rigs fell "from 17 to 13," while describing other basins as "flat" and attributing shifts to gas-price dynamics: "with natural gas prices disappointing this year... the Mid-Con... probably was less competitive for CapEx dollars." (CFO Ravnaas)

  • Paul Diamond, Citigroup Inc., Research Division: asked which basins/packages Kimbell prefers in 2H; President & CFO Ravnaas said, "We're always basin and commodity agnostic" but emphasized win-rate differences: "If we put out 25 bids, we maybe get 1" in Permian-only deals, while "we're more competitive on multi-basin portfolios." (CFO Ravnaas)

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts were slightly negative to pressing on liquidity, pricing discipline, and basin curtailment risk, including concerns like being "over 70% drawn" and asking about "curtailments in the Permian." (Rezvan; Diamond)

  • Management tone was positive and assertive in prepared remarks ("outstanding quarter," "records") and more tactical in Q&A, using firm positioning on capital discipline and deal selectivity: "we're not going to overpay" and "you won't see us make acquisitions that will increase our leverage profile." (CFO Ravnaas)

  • Versus Q1, management kept a similarly upbeat consolidation and activity message, but Q2 included sharper competitive color ("got absolutely destroyed") and more specific near-term transaction cadence around updating guidance post drop-down close. (CFO Ravnaas)

Quarter-over-quarter Comparison

  • Distribution increased to $0.47 from $0.41, while management maintained the same payout framework: "75% of cash available for distribution" to common unitholders and "the remaining 25%" toward revolver paydown. (CEO Ravnaas; CFO Ravnaas)

  • Scale and activity signals strengthened, with rigs rising to 91 from 85 and management highlighting "over $360 million in acquisitions over the last 90 days" after Q1 described evaluating packages with "nothing imminent to report." (CEO Ravnaas; CFO Ravnaas)

  • Balance sheet commentary shifted from Q1 net debt ratio "approximately 1.6x" to Q2 "approximately 1.4x," alongside a borrowing base increase to $660 million from $625 million. (CFO Ravnaas)

Risks and Concerns

  • "Oil prices have been especially volatile in recent weeks due to the stops and starts of the Middle East conflict" and management acknowledged broader "geopolitical" uncertainty while still expecting the forward strip to support activity. (CEO Ravnaas)

  • Acquisition-market risk centered on pricing and competition: "the Permian continues to be very hot" and Kimbell cited instances where bids were "nearly 2x" its level, with mitigation framed as selectivity and cost-of-capital discipline. (CFO Ravnaas)

  • Liquidity and preferred-redemption trade-offs were explicitly flagged, with mitigation tied to maintaining conservative leverage and opportunistic actions: "We may opportunistically go up very slightly to redeem additional preferred units." (CFO Ravnaas)

Final Takeaway

Management framed Q2 as a record quarter with $103 million of oil, natural gas, and NGL revenues and a $0.47 distribution, while emphasizing a near-term catalyst in the drop-down acquisition expected to close later in August and drive a subsequent guidance update. In Q&A, executives highlighted discipline on leverage and acquisition pricing amid intense Permian competition, pointing to expected added borrowing-base capacity post drop-down, continued selectivity in M&A, and an ongoing focus on maintaining liquidity while balancing preferred redemptions and capital returns.

data.title: Syntholene upsizes private placement to C$2.3M
data.description:
• Syntholene (SYNTF) increased its previously announced non-brokered private placement to C$2.3M due to strong investor demand.
  • The offering consists of up to 5.11M units at C$0.45/unit, with each unit including one common share and one-half warrant (full warrant exercisable at C$0.63 for 2 years).
  • Closing is expected around August 14, 2026.
  • Proceeds will fund testing and production at the company's Húsavík, Iceland demonstration facility and provide working capital.

data.title: AbCellera rises as it will release phase 2 results of menopause asset
data.description:
• AbCellera Biologics (ABCL) is up ~8% in after-hours trading following an announcement it will release top-line phase 2 data on ABCL635 for the moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms due to menopause before market open on August 10.
  • The double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial enrolled about 80 postmenopausal women.
  • "ABCL635 specifically targets NK3R, a clinically validated G protein-coupled receptor [GPCR] expressed on KNDy neurons in the infundibular nucleus of the hypothalamus," according to AbCellera.

data.title: Groupon expects Q3 billings growth of 4% to 6% while migrating all surfaces to new platform by end of Q3
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Groupon (GRPN) Q2 2026

Management View

  • CEO Dusan Senkypl said Q2 “fell slightly short on the top line with Billings and Revenue each down 1% year over year,” while “adjusted EBITDA finished at the high end of our guidance range and free cash flow was strong at a positive $15 million,” and he attributed the shortfall to North America Local pressure that “came in below our expectations.”
  • Senkypl emphasized Project Foundry as “our most consequential initiative” to make Groupon “an AI-native company,” adding, “Our ambition is that AI handles all repetitive work at Groupon,” and stating that “engineering output per developer has more than doubled in the past 6 months.”
  • On marketplace initiatives, Senkypl said “Revenue from our organic channels returned to growth in Q2,” and described trust/quality actions: “We are raising the bar on what appears on Groupon and have remediated or removed hundreds of deals that did not meet it.”
  • Senkypl announced leadership changes: “Adi Rajkumar joined Groupon as Chief Operating Officer, and Mark Marge joined as Vice President of Marketplace Strategy and Operations,” tying the hires to North America local supply that “has been running behind our expectations.”
  • CFO Rana Kashyap said July strength was broad-based: “we are seeing, I would say, broad-based strength across the platform,” including “Things To Do” and “Beauty and Wellness,” adding, “North America has picked up. But really, the comment we made was for the whole company.”

Outlook

  • Senkypl guided Q3 to “billing growth of 4% to 6%,” “Revenue of $128 million to $130 million,” “adjusted EBITDA of $19 million to $21 million and negative free cash flow in the quarter.”
  • For the full year, Senkypl said Groupon is “maintaining our outlook” of “Billings growth of 3% to 5%, revenue of $513 million to $523 million, adjusted EBITDA of $75 million to $80 million, and free cash flow of at least $60 million,” and added, “Our outlook implies second half revenue growth of approximately 6% at the low end and approximately 10% at the high end.”
  • Senkypl cautioned on execution risk embedded in the ramp: “The acceleration of our outlook requires -- runs ahead of our current pace, and a slower ramp across these drivers would affect our ability to reach it.”

Financial Results

  • Senkypl reported Q2 “Billings and Revenue each down 1% year over year,” and said Q2 adjusted EBITDA “finished at the high end of our guidance range” while “free cash flow was strong at a positive $15 million.”
  • Senkypl said performance diverged by area, with the “top-line shortfall… concentrated in North America Local,” while he pointed to early Q3 signal: “our business accelerating to mid-single-digit growth in July.”

Q&A

  • Robert Brooks, Northland Capital Markets: asked about new UI rollout because he still saw “the classic UI”; CEO Dusan Senkypl: said Groupon is in “the last phases of migration,” “cleaning up the last and least used parts,” and expects frequent personalization releases, adding the platform “unlocks a ton of new opportunities and the pace of development… is completely different.”
  • Robert Brooks, Northland Capital Markets: asked what KPIs track trust/quality progress; CEO Senkypl: “ultimate metric… is purchase frequency,” and cited “conversion to second purchase” plus a shift toward optimizing campaigns for “lifetime value.”
  • Robert Brooks, Northland Capital Markets: asked about the McDonald’s loyalty-app partnership and more such deals; CEO Senkypl: said “it was our first partnership of this type with McDonald’s,” and “my plan is to show more of these,” tying them to brand visibility and increased exposure.
  • Eric Sheridan, Goldman Sachs: asked what in June/July supports back-half framing and how much is macro vs. execution; CEO Senkypl: said comparisons ease, cited platform rollout progress, SEO/managed-channel improvement, higher second-half marketing, and stated, “we are not counting on macro… but I don't see macro as a headwind to us.”
  • Retail written question (Reddit): asked about inconsistent redemption/merchant quality and supply-side agentic initiatives; CEO Senkypl: said Groupon is “building curated marketplace where every deal earns its place,” described AI-driven pricing/complaint detection, and said, “The AI voice agent program for merchant outreach continues,” with an objective that “the majority of new merchant meetings [be] set by AI agents by the end of this year.”
  • Sean McGowan, ROTH: asked how Groupon communicates the trust/quality shift; CEO Senkypl: said, “we are trying to do the work first,” and only later expand marketing, potentially “through some types of guarantees.”
  • Sean McGowan, ROTH: asked for July strength by segment; CFO Rana Kashyap: said “broad-based strength across the platform,” with strength in “tours and attractions” and “local activity,” and reiterated the July comment was “for the whole company.”
  • Sean McGowan, ROTH: asked what’s attributable to Foundry; CEO Senkypl: said the sequence is internal operating change first, citing speedboats and data/AI access, and added, “I’m not able right now to share the expected numbers.”
  • Retail written question (X): asked about younger cohorts and evidence; CEO Senkypl: said influencer marketing will increase, a “different onboarding experience… rolled out completely in Q3,” cited viral traction in “tourist packages,” and said “active customers grew again this quarter.”
  • Robert Brooks, Northland Capital Markets: asked if North America local was high single digits in July; CFO Kashyap: “we're not going to start getting into the exact numbers,” but said “North America local did improve versus Q2,” and noted strength in North America Travel and that International “maintained the level.”
  • Retail written question (X): asked about subscription; CEO Senkypl: said Groupon has considered it, but “at this moment, we have really nothing to announce.”
  • Retail written question (X): asked about UGC/influencer content; CEO Senkypl: said Groupon is running experiments with “tens of millions of impressions,” and wants tools where influencers can select deals and “ask AI to build them their own… mini website.”

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts’ tone was slightly skeptical and detail-seeking, pressing on UI rollout visibility, segment-level July strength, and proof points for Foundry; CFO Kashyap declined extra granularity: “we're not going to start getting into the exact numbers.”
  • Management tone was slightly positive in prepared remarks and more explanatory in Q&A, with confidence anchored in execution cadence and AI progress; Senkypl said, “we enter Q3 with momentum,” while also flagging contingency: “a slower ramp… would affect our ability to reach it.”
  • Versus the prior quarter, management language shifted from Q1 underperformance (“Q1 fell short of our expectations”) toward traction signals (“mid-single-digit growth in July”), while analysts continued to probe the same core issues: North America local, marketing channels, and AI’s measurable impact.

Quarter-over-Quarter Comparison

  • Guidance posture tightened into explicit acceleration metrics: Q2 highlighted Q3 billings growth of 4% to 6% and reiterated full-year ranges, while Q1 framed second-half improvement more conditionally and guided Q2 within a narrower near-term range.
  • Strategic emphasis broadened: Q1 introduced Foundry and restructuring evaluation; Q2 focused on operational outcomes (hyperlocal campaigns at scale, faster support resolution) and added a new “Trust and quality” bet with deal removals and upcoming verification/redemption updates.
  • Leadership actions changed: Q2 added a COO and a marketplace strategy/ops VP to address North America local supply execution, a focus that was also a pressure point in Q1.
  • Analysts’ focus remained consistent on North America local recovery and AI proof points, while Q2 added more questions on trust/quality communication and onboarding younger users.

Risks and Concerns

  • Senkypl said Q2 top-line pressure was “concentrated in North America Local,” and noted execution dependency for the second-half ramp: “a slower ramp across these drivers would affect our ability to reach it.”
  • Senkypl characterized organic as “inherently volatile,” and described quality/trust as a trade-off where changes could create “slightly lower… conversion” but target “much lower refunds… and then… increased purchase frequency.”
  • CFO Kashyap declined to quantify July segment strength beyond directional comments, leaving investors dependent on future disclosures for confirmation of the pace in North America local.

Final Takeaway

Management framed Q2 as a modest top-line miss driven by North America Local but paired it with high-end adjusted EBITDA delivery, positive $15 million free cash flow, and an early Q3 signal of mid-single-digit July growth. The call centered on execution in the second half via Project Foundry’s AI-native operating shift, a near-complete platform migration expected by end of Q3, a stepped-up trust-and-quality push that includes removing subpar deals and adding pre-publication verification, and new leadership hires aimed at improving North America local supply performance, while reiterating full-year targets and warning that the implied acceleration requires a timely ramp in these drivers.

data.title: Serve Robotics forecasts $9M-$10M 2026 revenue amid plans not to renew Uber agreement in early 2027
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Serve Robotics (SERV) Q2 2026

Management view

  • CEO Ali Kashani said Q2 marked a break in a multi-year trend tied to Uber, noting, "From the first quarter of 2022 through the first quarter of this year, delivery volume through Uber grew for 17 consecutive quarters. In Q2, that trend reversed for the first time." He attributed the change to "lower than expected robot utilization" and added, "we believe the reversal in Q2 was largely due to the changes in the operating model and the integration between the two companies."

  • Kashani said Serve and Uber have "differing views about the operating model to scale our shared autonomous fleet" and concluded, "we don't currently expect that it would make sense to renew our agreements when it expires in early 2027." He added, "We will continue to engage with Uber and we are open to finding a path to continue working together," while emphasizing, "Ultimately, we need to focus our resources where we see the clearest path to high utilization and operational leverage."

  • Kashani reported Q2 revenue of "$3.2 million" and stated, "we are lowering our full year 2026 revenue guidance from $26 million to a range of $9 to $10 million." He framed the cut as removing future assumptions, saying, "The principal driver of this change is the removal of the delivery volume growth that we had assumed for the second half."

  • Kashani highlighted diversification, stating, "DoorDash, grew nearly 50% sequentially last quarter," and adding, "we'll be announcing another major delivery marketplace partner in the coming weeks." He also said, "Our advertising revenues accounted for nearly 50% of our robotic food delivery revenues last quarter" and "we have signed 7 multi-year contract extensions with our hospital customers and 2 new hospitals."

  • Kashani previewed product and market initiatives, saying, "On August 17, we plan to provide our 2026 summer announcement" spanning "a new delivery marketplace partnership, 2 new market launches, a merchant integration products and new technology advances." He introduced Beacon: "our new product, Beacon, is a standalone countertop device" and emphasized, "Because it has its own cellular connectivity, it requires nothing from the restaurant beyond a consistent source of power."

  • CFO Brian Read described the quarter as a reset: "This was a pivotal quarter for us," and added, "Strategically, we're positioning our offerings to pass more value directly to merchants and customers." He reiterated operating priorities: "make each robot more productive, grow revenue per robot and per hour, grow the recurring part of our revenue."

Outlook

  • CFO Read guided, "we're revising our full year 2026 revenue guidance to approximately $9 million to $10 million," and said the change reflects that "the delivery decline wasn't just a future impact" and that a prior second-half Uber ramp "is not materializing, and we've removed it from our outlook entirely."

  • Read updated spending plans, saying, "We've reduced planned 2026 capital expenditures from about $25 million down to approximately $15 million to $17 million" and "We're lowering our 2026 non-GAAP operating expense outlook from $160 million to $170 million down to approximately from $140 million to $150 million."

  • Compared with Q1 messaging, management previously said, "We reiterate a total 2026 revenue guidance of $26 million," while Q2 language shifted to, "The near-term revenue number is lower" after "hard, clarifying decisions" and a focus on "low-margin, low-control channels."

Financial results

  • CFO Read reported Q2 "total revenue" of "$3.2 million" and said it reflected "2 very different trends" because "Delivery revenue declined meaningfully" while "our other channels grew enough to more than offset it." He added, "Recurring revenue was over 50% of total revenue this quarter" and "software revenue was once again nearly $1 million."

  • Read reported profitability and cost structure metrics, stating, "Gross loss for the quarter was approximately $8.8 million, and gross margin was negative 271%," and adding, "Fleet gross margin improved sequentially even as we absorbed the Uber decline." He also reported, "GAAP operating expenses were $57.3 million in Q2," with "Non-GAAP operating expenses... approximately $40.4 million."

  • Read reported bottom-line and liquidity figures: "GAAP net loss for the quarter was $64 million, or negative $0.80 per share," and "Non-GAAP net loss was $47.1 million, or negative $0.59 per share." He added, "We ended the quarter with more than $240 million in cash and marketable securities."

Q&A

  • Mike Latimore, Northland Capital Markets: "can you just elaborate... what happened in the second quarter?" Ali Kashani: "there are a lot of investments happening on both sides into the platform" and "a lot of decisions are being made about how do you allocate orders, how do you organize fleets?... we were not perfectly aligned" and "we decided we should be transparent... that we don't believe that this would be kind of renewed."

  • Mike Latimore, Northland Capital Markets: asked which channel matters more and how direct-to-merchant would reach customers. Ali Kashani: "we want to have control over our destiny" and said DoorDash momentum continued, adding, "between June and July, we grew another 50%." He also said Serve will invest in channels "that allows us to work with anybody directly" and "pass a lot of the value to restaurants and customers directly."

  • Mike Latimore, Northland Capital Markets: asked about software revenue in 2H and Diligent. Brian Read: "from a software standpoint, it will be a little softer in the back half" and "the strength of Diligent... will continue," adding, "we're not going to get into the split between Diligent."

  • Colin Rusch, Oppenheimer: asked about autonomy efficiency KPIs and learning cadence. Ali Kashani: "the most important KPI is are the robots getting better... faster... safer... more reliable" and said, "Once we share more about the new generation autonomy, we would have more color."

  • Jeffrey Cohen, Ladenburg Thalmann: asked about advertising mix, pricing, and forward view. Ali Kashani: "we see both local and national campaigns right now" and "something like 50% of our sidewalk revenue came from advertising." Brian Read: "they're mostly wraps" and cited "growth within the experiential side of the business," but said, "not something we get into for guiding to advertising versus deliveries."

  • Jeffrey Cohen, Ladenburg Thalmann: asked about non-food (NoScrubs) and geographies. Ali Kashani: "one of them that we announced recently was NoScrubs. This is laundry" and added, "we are not building robots to just deliver burritos. This is last-mile infrastructure for cities."

Sentiment analysis

  • Slightly negative analyst tone centered on utilization and revenue durability, with direct probing such as, "Why do you think utilization was not hitting goals?" and repeated requests for segmentation and forward visibility.

  • Management tone was slightly defensive but controlled around Uber specifics, with Ali Kashani saying, "needless to say, I want to be respectful of partner confidentiality," while remaining confident on diversification and product roadmap, including, "we feel really good about the potential for revenue to scale."

  • Versus Q1’s more optimistic framing ("on track to deliver the $26 million"), Q2 included more cautionary language ("hard, clarifying decisions") while maintaining emphasis on autonomy investment and multi-channel monetization.

Quarter-over-quarter comparison

  • Q2 introduced a specific partnership inflection: "In Q2, that trend reversed" in Uber volume, and Serve said it "do[es] not currently believe" it will renew the Uber agreement in early 2027; Q1 had emphasized platform expansion with partners "besides Uber and DoorDash" without signaling non-renewal.

  • Full-year revenue guidance shifted from Q1’s "We reiterate a total 2026 revenue guidance of $26 million" to Q2’s "$9 million to $10 million," alongside tighter capital plans and lower non-GAAP OpEx guidance.

  • Analyst focus moved from market expansion/regulatory pipeline (Q1) toward root-causing utilization, channel strategy, and second-half softness (Q2), with management repeatedly emphasizing allocation toward "high utilization" and "better economics."

Risks and concerns

  • Management cited partner operating-model risk and integration friction, stating the Q2 reversal was "largely due to the changes in the operating model and the integration between the two companies" and that alignment on "fleet coordination or merchant integration" is necessary to scale.

  • Advertising demand risk was described as "headwinds of geopolitical macro pressure on advertising spending," with CFO Read adding, "we're going to see the continued headwinds" and expecting software to be "a little softer" in the second half.

  • Execution risk around reallocation was acknowledged implicitly as the company shifts away from assumptions tied to Uber ramp; management’s mitigation centered on redeploying capacity, saying, "our robots can be deployed to direct merchant relationships, other verticals and the new delivery marketplace platform."

Final takeaway

Serve’s Q2 call centered on a material reset to 2026 expectations after Uber-related utilization fell short, prompting management to cut full-year revenue guidance to $9 million-$10 million and signal that it does not currently expect to renew the Uber agreement in early 2027 absent operating-model changes. Management emphasized that Q2 revenue still grew sequentially due to diversification, highlighting advertising, hospital robotics recurring contracts, DoorDash growth, and near-term product and partnership announcements (including Beacon) as the pathway to higher utilization and improved unit economics, while tightening OpEx and capex plans for the second half.

data.title: Sanuwave withdraws FY2026 revenue guidance amid CMS proposal implying 97610 reimbursement of $316.59 in 2027
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: SANUWAVE Health (SNWV) Q2 2026

Management View

  • "Q2 actually started out fairly strong, and applicator sales remained so during the whole quarter, setting a new all-time record for both unit volumes, up 13% sequentially from our previous record in Q1 and 27% year-over-year, and for applicator revenues, up 8% sequentially from Q1... These were up 13% year-over-year." (CEO & Chairman Morgan Frank)
  • "Where Q2 meaningfully diverged from plan and expectation was on the system sales side... this has created an unprecedented market for used UltraMIST devices, which wound up having profound cannibalization effects on our business during the quarter." (CEO & Chairman Frank)
  • "So our best guess is that used systems accounted for 40 to 60 system sales in the quarter... it's difficult to be precise." (CEO & Chairman Frank)
  • "Our count for active systems at the end of Q2 was 1,411, up 29 from the 1,382 at the end of Q1." (CEO & Chairman Frank)
  • "We did get some positive news from the calendar year 2027 Hospital Outpatient Prospective Payment System proposed rule... [it] proposes to increase reimbursement for UltraMIST by 14% for 2027 when used in the hospital outpatient setting." (CEO & Chairman Frank)
  • "If... this rule were to go into effect, our read is that reimbursement for UltraMIST would drop from its present $397 average to approximately $316 in 2027, with further reductions to follow in 2028." (CEO & Chairman Frank)
  • "Revenue for the second quarter came in at $9.7 million, a decrease of 3% versus $10.1 million in the prior year quarter... the softness was concentrated in capital or system sales, while the recurring core applicator business held up well." (CFO & Secretary Peter Sorensen)

Outlook

  • "With regard to guidance, we're going to adopt a cautious stance here... SANUWAVE is withdrawing its previously issued fiscal year 2026 revenue guidance, which should no longer be relied upon." (CEO & Chairman Morgan Frank)
  • "The company will not provide quarterly or annual guidance until there is greater clarity on these topics and expects to reassess this after CMS publishes its final rule, which is anticipated in the fourth quarter of 2026." (CEO & Chairman Frank)
  • "The comment period runs through September 14, and we expect the final rule to be announced in or around the first week of November." (CEO & Chairman Frank)

Financial Results

  • "Revenue for the 3 months ended June 30, 2026, totaled $9.7 million... The year-over-year decrease was driven by lower UltraMIST system revenue, which declined approximately 34% to $2.3 million from $3.4 million." (CFO & Secretary Peter Sorensen)
  • "On a reported basis, our consumables, parts, and accessories line... increased approximately 12% to $7.3 million from $6.5 million." (CFO & Secretary Sorensen)
  • "Gross margin as a percentage of revenue... was 76.2%... The decline was driven primarily by a shift in revenue mix toward consumables and away from higher-margin system sales, together with lower average selling prices..." (CFO & Secretary Sorensen)
  • "Operating loss... totaled $0.3 million... OPEX for the quarter were $7.7 million compared to $6.4 million in the prior year quarter." (CFO & Secretary Sorensen)
  • "Net loss... was $0.7 million, compared to net income of $0.6 million" and "Cash and cash equivalents totaled $9.4 million" with "$2.9 million in scheduled principal payments on our term loan." (CFO & Secretary Sorensen)

Q&A

  • Sean Westropp, Deep Sail Capital: asked for a customer breakdown between for-profit/mobile wound care vs. hospital and other settings; CEO & Chairman Frank said "we have a lot of customers whose models are hybrid" and "the delineation is not as sharp as you might expect," adding that with hospital groups "these customers tend to be slower to ramp up, but kind of have that sort of supertanker momentum once they get going."
  • Sean Westropp, Deep Sail Capital: asked for more detail behind the implied $316 reimbursement estimate; CEO & Chairman Frank said "we believe [the conversion factor] is going to be 32.84 in 2027" and walked through RVUs, concluding "that gets us to an estimate of $316.59."
  • Sean Westropp, Deep Sail Capital: asked about timing and feedback on the resubmission/comment process; CEO & Chairman Frank said "There's a 60-day comment period" that "ends on September 14" and "the final rule will likely be announced in or around the first week of November."

Sentiment Analysis

  • "Can you just give us a little more color on how you're getting to the 316 number?" and "is there any indications on when you will get any feedback on that" reflected a slightly negative/skeptical analyst tone centered on reimbursement math and process timing. (Sean Westropp, Deep Sail Capital)
  • Management tone was slightly negative on capital equipment demand but more confident on consumables and the policy response, including "we're going to try very, very hard" and "we believe that there is a strong case to be made" during prepared remarks, then more technical and matter-of-fact in Q&A when detailing RVUs and the conversion factor. (CEO & Chairman Morgan Frank)
  • Versus Q1, management moved from Q1’s "We are maintaining our guidance of $51 million to $55 million for the year" to Q2’s "withdrawing" guidance language, while the Q2 Q&A narrowed to reimbursement mechanics rather than Q1’s broader confidence discussion about second-half growth. (CEO & Chairman Frank)

Quarter-over-quarter Comparison

  • Q2 introduced a new headwind absent from Q1’s prepared remarks: "an unprecedented market for used UltraMIST devices" with "profound cannibalization effects" and an estimate that "used systems accounted for 40 to 60 system sales in the quarter." (CEO & Chairman Morgan Frank)
  • Q2 guidance posture reversed from Q1’s "Our guidance for Q2 is 10% to 15% year-on-year growth... We are maintaining our guidance of $51 million to $55 million for the year" to Q2’s "withdrawing its previously issued fiscal year 2026 revenue guidance." (CEO & Chairman Frank)
  • Financial mix and profitability narrative shifted from Q1’s "We delivered the highest Q1 revenues in company history" to Q2’s "Revenue... $9.7 million, a decrease of 3%" with the decline "concentrated in capital or system sales" and system revenue down to "$2.3 million." (CFO & Secretary Peter Sorensen)

Risks and Concerns

  • "Wound care has been quite a market over the last 12 months" and CMS skin-sub reimbursement changes and "Clawbacks on past payments have sucked huge amounts of money out of the space," which management tied to customer closures and the used-system supply. (CEO & Chairman Morgan Frank)
  • "97610 was nominated as a mispriced code" and, if finalized, would imply a drop "from its present $397 average to approximately $316 in 2027"; management’s mitigation was "both we and a great number of UltraMIST users... plan to participate in this comment period" and "seek a meeting with CMS." (CEO & Chairman Frank)
  • "Operating loss" and higher expenses were discussed alongside mitigation language: "we remain focused on disciplined cost management and expect operating leverage to improve as revenue scales." (CFO & Secretary Peter Sorensen)

Final Takeaway

SANUWAVE’s Q2 message centered on a split between record applicator performance and unexpectedly weak system sales, which management attributed to broad provider stress and a surge in used UltraMIST devices that "cannibaliz[ed]" new sales. The company shifted its investor framing around reimbursement risk, citing a proposed 2027 HOPPS increase of 14% in hospital outpatient settings but also detailing a Physician Fee Schedule proposal that could reduce 97610 reimbursement to an estimated $316.59. Against that uncertainty, management withdrew FY2026 revenue guidance and said it will reassess after CMS’s final rule, which it expects in early November following the September 14 comment deadline.

data.title: Trulieve anticipates at least $225M in 2026 operating cash flow while raising capex outlook to $95M
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Trulieve Cannabis Corp. (TRLV) Q2 2026

Management View

  • “We are thrilled to report second quarter results for the first time as a company listed on the New York Stock Exchange.” (Founder, Chairman & CEO Kimberly Rivers)

  • “In April, Attorney General Todd Blanche rescheduled state-licensed medical marijuana to Schedule III… [and] the Treasury Department confirmed that punitive 280E tax no longer applies to state-licensed medical marijuana operations beginning in 2026.” (CEO Rivers)

  • “In order to facilitate listing on the New York Stock Exchange, Trulieve segregated the medical-only, state-licensed DEA-registered business from the mixed-use states… Following precedent and as part of the deconsolidation, 10% of the mixed-use business was sold to an independent third-party investor along with operational control.” (CEO Rivers)

  • “Second quarter revenue of $271 million was in line with guidance… Second quarter gross margin of 60%… Adjusted EBITDA of $98 million, or 36% margin… we generated $53 million in operating cash flow, which contributed to our quarter-end cash balance of $325 million.” (CEO Rivers)

  • “Second quarter net loss was $406 million, which includes a $407 million impact from the Harvest deconsolidation and equity investment. Excluding non-recurring items, second quarter net income would have been $20 million or $0.11 per share.” (Chief Financial Officer Jan Reese)

Outlook

  • “Third quarter revenue will include only Trulieve's medical operations. We expect third quarter revenue to be comparable to the medical-only revenue of $222 million in the second quarter.” (CFO Reese)

  • “Gross margin is expected to be comparable to the 63% gross margin in the second quarter for the medical-only operations.” (CFO Reese)

  • “For the full year 2026, we anticipate operating cash flow of at least $225 million, reduced from $250 million to reflect the impact of deconsolidation.” (CFO Reese)

  • “Capital expenditures are now expected to be $95 million, up from $85 million. Pending regulatory approvals, we may accelerate investment in Texas.” (CFO Reese)

Financial Results

  • “Second quarter gross profit totaled $162 million or 60% margin… Second quarter SG&A was $102 million or 38% of revenue.” (CFO Reese)

  • “We ended the quarter with $325 million in cash and $289 million in debt… Capital expenditures were $21 million. And free cash flow totaled $32 million.” (CFO Reese)

  • “In June, the company adopted a share repurchase program of up to the lesser of $50 million or approximately 8.5 million shares. During the second quarter, no shares were repurchased.” (CFO Reese)

Q&A

  • Luke Hannan, Canaccord Genuity Corp., Research Division: “Should we think about Trulieve's presence in Georgia… primarily through its own dispensary network or… the pharmacy channel?” CEO Rivers: “That network will be expanding, and we will wholesale to those folks… [and] there’s also interesting opportunities… to do a hybrid model… ‘store within a store’… a JV… Or there’s also an opportunity for us to purchase independent pharmacies.”

  • Luke Hannan, Canaccord Genuity Corp., Research Division: On Texas scale, “is it reasonable to assume that you should try and get to that same level of scale in Texas…?” CEO Rivers: “Absolutely. We are very laser focused on the Texas opportunity… Texas regulators have been notified that we are ready for inspections… and… we will be moving very quickly as soon as we get the green light that our license has converted to final.”

  • Luke Hannan, Canaccord Genuity Corp., Research Division: On hemp conversion tailwinds, “what could be the organic revenue tailwinds… from folks converting from the hemp markets…?” CEO Rivers: “We estimate… about 7,000 [hemp storefronts] in Florida… The regulated medical marijuana market… is about $2 billion. And the hemp market in Florida… about $4 billion… [and] in Texas… about a $6 billion market.”

  • Aaron Grey, Alliance Global Partners, Research Division: On Georgia supply, “how best to think about… long-term supply… given… additional distribution outlets through pharmacies.” CEO Rivers: “As a Tier 1 license holder, we have the ability to expand up to 100,000 square feet of canopy… and… Georgia is very invested in the success of this program… [which] is going to require… supply of high quality product.”

  • Gabrielle Ingoglia, Cantor Fitzgerald & Co., Research Division: “Does the $222 million revenue guidance for Q3 '26 incorporate… sales ramp back up… [in Georgia]?” CEO Rivers: “Guidance would incorporate our estimates… rebound in Georgia… [and] in late Q3, that shortage will be rectified and sales will restart… full contribution coming in Q4.”

  • William Kirk, ROTH Capital Partners, LLC, Research Division: “How the uplisting has changed your conversations with capital market participants…?” CEO Rivers: “We have been having active conversations… with some of the bulge bracket guys… cannabis prohibitions… they’re working through committees… and I am confident that we will have… additional institutional investors… in the next 12 months.”

  • Frederico Yokota Gomes, ATB Cormark Capital Markets Inc., Research Division: On CapEx and M&A, “Any specific market or project… driving… increase?” CFO Reese: “One of those strategic opportunities… is obviously Georgia… [and] as the opportunity arises… we will double down… in Texas.” CEO Rivers: “We are absolutely inquisitive as it relates to M&A… we are listed on NYSE… [which is] an attractive setup… as long as it makes sense and fits into our criteria.”

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts’ tone was slightly positive and opportunity-focused, pressing mainly on execution details in Georgia and Texas (supply, market structure, and guidance assumptions), including “how best to think about… long-term supply” (Aaron Grey, Alliance Global Partners, Research Division) and “does the $222 million revenue guidance… incorporate” Georgia’s ramp (Gabrielle Ingoglia, Cantor Fitzgerald & Co., Research Division).

  • Management’s tone was positive and expansion-forward, repeatedly emphasizing speed and readiness around catalysts, including “we will be moving very quickly as soon as we get the green light” (CEO Rivers) and “we anticipate operating cash flow of at least $225 million” (CFO Reese).

  • Prior-quarter transcript was not provided, so tone changes versus last quarter were not available from the materials.

Quarter-over-quarter Comparison

  • The previous-quarter earnings call transcript was not available in the provided materials, so quarter-over-quarter changes in guidance language, strategy emphasis, and Q&A focus could not be assessed.

Risks and Concerns

  • “We expect quarterly gross margin to vary based on product and market mix, inventory sell-through, promotional activities and idle capacity costs.” (CFO Reese)

  • CEO Rivers described near-term execution risk in Georgia tied to product availability: “In Q3… we had a great start, and then we have… a shortage… [and] in late Q3, that shortage will be rectified.”

  • On regulatory timing, CEO Rivers framed a key dependency for Texas scaling: “we will be moving very quickly as soon as we get the green light that our license has converted to final.”

Final Takeaway

Management emphasized that Q2 reflected a major structural shift—NYSE listing enabled by deconsolidating Harvest—alongside a federal policy backdrop that removed 280E for state-licensed medical marijuana beginning in 2026. They tied the near-term setup to a flat Q3 revenue outlook for the medical-only business versus Q2 medical-only revenue, with Georgia and Pennsylvania expected to offset typical Florida seasonality, while raising full-year investment plans (capex) and framing Texas as a fast-moving, large-scale medical opportunity pending final licensing and regulatory approvals.

data.title: Concentra targets $2.325B-$2.375B 2026 revenue and $485M-$495M adjusted EBITDA as CEO transition set for November 1
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Concentra Group Holdings Parent, Inc. (CON) Q2 2026

Management View

  • "After more than a decade as Concentra's Chief Executive Officer... I have decided effective November 1 of this year to transition from the CEO role into a new role at Concentra as its Executive Chairman of the Board." (CEO & Director William Newton). Newton added, "At that time, Matt Dicanio, our President and Chief Financial Officer, will become Concentra's President and Chief Executive Officer," and described the handoff as "the result of a multi-year succession plan."
  • "This transition reflects continuity... the strategy we've articulated since our IPO... is working, and it will not change on November 1." (President & CFO Matthew DiCanio). DiCanio also highlighted operating momentum, saying "total company revenue was $606 million" and "adjusted EBITDA was $140.9 million," while pointing to volume and pricing, including "total occupational health center patient visits increased 2.6%" and "revenue per visit grew 4.6%."
  • "We believe that this reflects both the resilient blue-collar labor market where we generally operate as well as market share gains." (President & CFO DiCanio). He tied share gains to commercial execution, noting, "we are continuing to deploy new tactics and technologies" and said customer "satisfaction and retention metrics remaining at or near all-time highs."
  • "We are substantially complete with our efforts" to separate from Select Medical, including that the company "largely finalized all process and technology implementations, including the conversion of our ERP system to our own instance in May of this year." (CEO & Director Newton). He added, "Our monthly spend on TSA services Select Medical... will be entirely eliminated by November when the agreement officially ends."

Outlook

  • "Given the continued strength of the business, we are once again raising our 2026 guidance" to revenue of "$2.325 billion to $2.375 billion," adjusted EBITDA of "$485 million to $495 million," and free cash flow of "$220 million to $240 million," while "CapEx range of $70 million to $80 million remains unchanged." (CEO & Director Newton).
  • Management characterized the back-half setup in line with longer-term assumptions: "we continue to talk about the second half of the year similar to how we talk about our long-term algorithm, low single-digit visit growth, 3% rate growth." (President & CFO DiCanio). He also said, "there's -- could potentially be a little conservatism in the outlook," and added, "it's definitely not something we're seeing" in terms of demand weakening.

Financial Results

  • Q2 profitability and margins were framed as reflecting operating leverage: "adjusted EBITDA margin increased nearly 240 basis points... to 23.3%, reflecting strong rate and volume growth, coupled with good execution and operational efficiencies across the business." (President & CFO DiCanio). He also cited a prior-year headwind reversal: "Q2 2025 included just under $4 million of estimated Nova acquisition-related costs tied to onetime integration activities... eliminated through synergies."
  • Segment performance included: "total revenue of $553.5 million" in Occupational Health, "Onsite Health clinics... revenue of $38.8 million," and "other businesses... generated revenue of $13.7 million." (President & CFO DiCanio). On acquisitions, he said, "Both our Pivot and Nova acquisitions continue to perform very well and are ahead of underwriting."
  • Balance sheet and capital allocation updates included: "we generated $135.2 million in operating cash flow" and "free cash flow... totaled $121 million." (President & CFO DiCanio). He added, "we repurchased approximately 424,000 shares totaling $11 million" and "paid $8 million in dividends," with "approximately $54 million remaining" under the repurchase authorization.
  • Leverage and interest expense were positioned as near-term financial tailwinds: "Our net leverage ratio... was just under 3x, down from 3.4x at the end of the first quarter," and "we expect the interest rate spread on our Term Loan B to step down 25 basis points." (President & CFO DiCanio).

Q&A

  • Ann Hynes, Mizuho Securities USA LLC, Research Division: asked if the guidance raise reflects conservatism and what could drive long-term work comp growth; President & CFO DiCanio replied "we've raised our guidance by more than our beat" and reiterated "low single-digit visit growth, 3% rate growth," while adding the company is seeing "early signs" tied to "manufacturing and construction" and "the data center trend."
  • Joanna Gajuk, BofA Securities, Research Division: pressed on margin durability and drivers; President & CFO DiCanio answered, "Q2 and Q3 are the highest margin quarters" and said the company "do[es] anticipate the margins to move up" over time as separation costs roll off and scale benefits continue, while CEO & Director Newton added, "seasonality will take a little bit of the impact on the second half of the year."
  • Justin Bowers, Deutsche Bank AG, Research Division: asked about sustained above-trend work comp and market share runway; CEO & Director Newton said, "we really had a strong year" and attributed momentum to "tailwinds in the industry, combined with the market share gains," adding, "there's a lot of white space for us" and citing "over 200,000 small customers."
  • Stephen Baxter, Wells Fargo Securities, LLC, Research Division: asked about initial-injury mix sustainability and M&A pipeline size; President & CFO DiCanio said initial injuries "can fluctuate" but linked strength to "higher retention and overall market share gains," while CEO & Director Newton said, "As far as anything the size of Nova, that's not going to happen" and referenced "several nice midsized ones."
  • Scott Fidel, Goldman Sachs Group, Inc., Research Division: asked about strategic focus under the incoming CEO and free-cash-flow sustainability; President & CFO DiCanio responded, "no plans to change anything" and described Q2 free cash flow as benefiting from "some timing" and CapEx phasing, while reiterating expectation for "a very strong free cash flow year, well north of $200-plus million."
  • Benjamin Rossi, JPMorgan Chase & Co, Research Division: asked about center-level efficiency levers and Employer Services mix; CEO & Director Newton pointed to labor and throughput, saying Concentra improved "patient visits per FTE" via "technologies" that "eliminate... nonclinical activities," while President & CFO DiCanio said the company does not "really get into the breakdown" of Employer Services sub-lines.

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts’ tone was slightly positive, with multiple congratulations and questions focused on durability and conservatism, including "are you just being conservative?" (Ann Hynes, Mizuho Securities USA LLC, Research Division) and "how should we think about EBITDA margins going forward?" (Joanna Gajuk, BofA Securities, Research Division).
  • Management’s tone was positive and confident on operating momentum and continuity, emphasizing "nothing that we're seeing" in terms of demand deterioration (President & CFO DiCanio) and "we are substantially complete" on separation execution (CEO & Director Newton).
  • Versus Q1, management commentary shifted from weather/contextual drivers to sustained share gains and structural execution, while Q2 analysts increased focus on margin durability, leverage trajectory, and guidance conservatism.

Quarter-over-Quarter Comparison

  • Leadership and governance were the major change in Q2, with the company announcing a CEO transition effective November 1; Q1 did not include a CEO succession announcement.
  • Guidance language tightened upward again in Q2 (higher revenue, adjusted EBITDA, and free cash flow ranges), following a prior upward revision in Q1; Q2 management also characterized the second-half outlook as aligned with a "low single-digit" volume and "3%" rate framework (President & CFO DiCanio).
  • Operationally, Q2 highlighted a step-up in Employer Services growth rate discussion and stronger margin seasonality framing ("Q2 and Q3 are the highest margin quarters"), while Q1 highlighted the California rate timing and noted Tennessee would be meaningful in Q2.
  • Analyst focus shifted from Q1 topics like weather and New York rate updates to Q2 debates around margin sustainability, initial-injury mix, leverage milestones, and the strategic implications of the CEO transition.

Risks and Concerns

  • Management emphasized uncertainty around sustainability and timing of certain drivers, noting it is "still a little early to definitively point towards reshoring as a key driver" (President & CFO DiCanio) and that initial injuries "can fluctuate" (President & CFO DiCanio).
  • Seasonality was repeatedly cited as a margin headwind in the back half: "Q2 and Q3 are the highest margin quarters" (President & CFO DiCanio) and "seasonality will take a little bit of the impact" (CEO & Director Newton).
  • Capital deployment trade-offs remained in view, with management prioritizing "M&A, de novos" alongside "share repurchases" and the dividend, while maintaining a leverage objective of "in the range of 2.5x" (President & CFO DiCanio).

Final Takeaway

Concentra’s management framed Q2 as a quarter of operating momentum and transition planning: Newton set a November 1 CEO handoff to DiCanio while positioning the strategy as unchanged, and the team raised full-year 2026 guidance across revenue, adjusted EBITDA, and free cash flow. Prepared remarks and Q&A emphasized market share gains, resilient blue-collar demand, strong onsite growth, separation work nearing completion by November, and faster deleveraging to just under 3x with an expected step-down in term-loan pricing.

data.title: FIGS expects ~20% 2026 revenue growth while raising operating margin outlook to ~10.8%
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: FIGS, Inc. (FIGS) Q2 2026

Management View

  • “Net revenues grew 29% to $197 million, beating our outlook and marking our third straight quarter with 25% plus growth,” said (Co-Founder, CEO & Director Catherine Spear), adding that growth was “across our business rather than from just one part of it,” with record highs in scrubwear and each of “international, Teams and community hubs.”
  • Spear highlighted customer and spend metrics: “Active customer growth surged 13% to 3.1 million. AOV hit its own record of $127…[driving] net revenues per active customer to an all-time high…of $229.”
  • On capital return and confidence, Spear said: “We have not only accelerated our share buyback efforts during the quarter, but just announced a new $100 million authorization.”
  • Spear disclosed a supply-chain disruption: “U.S. Customs and Border Protection recently issued a withhold release order that currently prevents us from importing products into the United States from our partner in Jordan,” while adding, “we are able to raise our top and bottom line targets.”
  • “Q2 net revenues increased 29% year-over-year to $196.6 million,” said (Chief Financial Officer Sarah Oughtred), and “gross margin…improvement to 75.2%” included “the 780 basis point cumulative impact from the $15.4 million tariff refund.”

Outlook

  • “Our full year 2026 net revenues are now expected to grow approximately 20%, ahead of our prior outlook of 14% to 16% growth,” Oughtred said, adding the company is “planning for Q3 net revenue growth of approximately 20%…and Q4…approximately 10%.”
  • Oughtred said full-year GAAP gross margin is expected to “approximate 69.5%, inclusive of the tariff refund… and the expected benefit as impacted goods in inventory are sold,” while noting “the underlying gross margin expectation is unchanged from our prior guide.”
  • On profitability targets, Oughtred said: “We have increased our full year operating margin outlook…to approximately 10.8% inclusive of refunds” and “adjusted EBITDA margin…to between 14.8% and 15%.”

Financial Results

  • Oughtred said the quarter’s category mix and geography were led by “scrubwear grew 27%, representing 82% of net revenues,” and “non-scrubwear surged 40%, representing 18%,” while “U.S. net revenues increased 22% to $158.7 million” and “international…increased 67% to $37.9 million.”
  • On earnings and margins, Oughtred reported: “Net income for the quarter totaled $28.4 million or diluted EPS of $0.15,” and “operating margin…was 17.9% compared to 6.5% last year.”
  • On tariffs, Oughtred said: “Based on initial receipts of $4.5 million in Q2…[we] included the full benefit in our GAAP results,” and “subsequently, we have received the full amount of the refund in Q3.”
  • On liquidity and inventory, Oughtred said the company ended with “net cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments of $296.3 million,” and “inventory decreased 12% year-over-year to $119.6 million.”

Q&A

  • Robert Drbul, BTIG: asked what is working across new/returning customers; (CEO Spear) said it is “our 2 North Stars…product and marketing,” with “word of mouth” and a “replenishment-driven industry” bringing customers back.
  • Brian Nagel, Oppenheimer: asked about lapsed customers returning; (CFO Oughtred) said growth is coming from “new customers…lapsed customers… and…frequency of our returning customers.”
  • Nagel, Oppenheimer: asked if tariff refunds change strategy; (CFO Oughtred) said “we’re not earmarking it for anything specific…[and] continue to deliver returns for our shareholders.”
  • Brooke Roach, Goldman Sachs: asked about V Coterie expanding TAM; (CEO Spear) said “we have acquired V Coterie,” calling it “a TAM creation opportunity” and noting “we’ve sold out of a number of key styles.”
  • Matt Koranda, ROTH: asked AOV drivers and what’s embedded in guidance; (CFO Oughtred) said AOV reflected “pricing…lower discounts and improved returns,” and that frequency could be “an opportunity” beyond plan.
  • Ashley Owens, KeyBanc: asked Jordan WRO mitigation and in-stocks; (CEO Spear) said FIGS is “leveraging capacity with many of our other strong partners” and has “mitigated the vast, vast majority of the challenge.”
  • Nathaniel Feather, Morgan Stanley: asked international marketing balance; (CFO Oughtred) said the approach is “go broad and go deep,” with “full funnel marketing” in go-deep markets and testing lower funnel in go-broad markets.

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts sentiment was slightly positive, with repeated congratulatory framing (“spectacular quarter,” “phenomenal results”) while concentrating diligence on sustainability, tariffs, and the Jordan disruption.
  • Management sentiment was positive in prepared remarks and remained confident in Q&A, with Spear emphasizing “we are able to raise our top and bottom line targets,” and Oughtred calling the margin guide “a fairly clean base.”
  • Versus last quarter, management language shifted from caution on uncertain costs to higher certainty around 2026 targets, after incorporating tariff refund impacts into reported results and guidance.

Quarter-over-quarter Comparison

  • Guidance changed materially: Q1 called for full-year revenue growth of “14% to 16%,” while Q2 increased to “approximately 20%,” and operating margin moved from “between 7.8% and 8%” to “approximately 10.8% inclusive of refunds.”
  • New strategic developments in Q2 included “acquired V Coterie” and the Jordan “withhold release order,” while Q1 emphasized initiatives like the “Healthcare Human Act” and building Teams tech with a newly launched “Team store.”
  • Analysts’ focus broadened from Q1 topics (pricing elasticity, sourcing mix) to Q2 sustainability questions around customer reactivation, margin durability post-refunds, and supply continuity under the WRO.

Risks and Concerns

  • Supply chain risk was centered on Spear’s disclosure that the WRO “prevents us from importing…from our partner in Jordan,” with mitigation described as “leveraging capacity with our other…partners” and “expediting their production.”
  • Margin pressure offsets were flagged by Oughtred, including “use airfreight to expedite certain products,” and gross margin volatility in the second half, with “a year-over-year decline in Q3.”

Final Takeaway

FIGS management framed Q2 as broad-based acceleration, citing 29% revenue growth to $196.6 million, record customer economics, and a raised full-year outlook to ~20% revenue growth with higher operating and adjusted EBITDA margin targets. Alongside the $100 million buyback authorization and the V Coterie acquisition, management emphasized supply-chain agility in response to the Jordan WRO, while incorporating tariff refund impacts into reported results and the updated 2026 guidance.

data.title: U.S. drilling rig count stays flat in latest Baker Hughes weekly survey
data.description:
The number of oil and gas rigs actively drilling in the U.S. remained unchanged at 588, Baker Hughes said Friday in its latest weekly report.

The number of active drilling rigs targeting crude oil in the U.S. rose by 3 to 454 in the week ended August 7, while gas rigs dropped 3 to 124, and 10 rigs were classified as miscellaneous.

The total rig count was up 49, or 9%, compared to the same time last year, while the number of rigs drilling for oil rose by 43, or 10.4%, from a year ago, and gas rigs were up by 1 from a year earlier.

Rigs targeting oil in the Permian Basin gained 3 to 261, while oil rigs in the Eagle Ford and the Williston Basin stayed flat at 41 and 27, respectively.

ETFs: (USO), (UCO), (SCO), (USL), (DBO), (DRIP), (GUSH), (USOI), (UNG), (BOIL), (KOLD), (UNL), (FCG), (XLE)
